title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Exploring the data

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass_g) |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))

penguins_clean

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Average body mass by species

average_mass <- penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g))

average_mass

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_body_mass_g
  <fct>                <dbl>
1 Adelie               3701.
2 Chinstrap            3733.
3 Gentoo               5076.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Body mass comparison

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  )







Figure 1: Body mass distribution of Palmer Penguins by species.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Findings
The results show differences in body mass among the three penguin species. Gentoo penguins have a higher average body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. The boxplot also shows the distribution of body mass within each species.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Starting the MDS program at UBC has been both exciting and challenging. During orientation, I was excited to meet my classmates and learn more about the program, but I also felt a little overwhelmed by how fast-paced everything seemed. Coming from a life sciences background, I knew that learning programming and new technical tools would be a big part of this journey.
The first weeks of classes have introduced me to Python, R, statistics, and many new tools and concepts. One thing that surprised me most was the pace of the program. There is a lot to learn in a short amount of time, and some of the labs have been challenging, but each time I work through a problem I feel that I am making progress.
I am still adjusting to the intensity of the program, but I am becoming more comfortable with the material every day. I know there will be many challenges ahead, but I am excited to continue developing my skills and see how much I can learn throughout the MDS program.



Orientation day on campus.

title: Palmer Penguins with R and Python
text:
In this post, I use both R and Python to explore the Palmer Penguins dataset. I will prepare the data in R and then use Python to summarize and visualize the results.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: Palmer Penguins with R and Python
text:
Prepare the data in R

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)

penguins_r <- penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass_g) |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))

penguins_r

# A tibble: 342 × 2
   species body_mass_g
   <fct>         <int>
 1 Adelie         3750
 2 Adelie         3800
 3 Adelie         3250
 4 Adelie         3450
 5 Adelie         3650
 6 Adelie         3625
 7 Adelie         4675
 8 Adelie         3475
 9 Adelie         4250
10 Adelie         3300
# ℹ 332 more rows

title: Palmer Penguins with R and Python
section: Analyze the R data with Python
text:
Analyze the R data with Python

import pandas as pd

penguins_python = r.penguins_r

average_mass = (
    penguins_python
    .groupby("species", as_index=False)["body_mass_g"]
    .mean()
)

average_mass

     species  body_mass_g
0     Adelie  3700.662252
1  Chinstrap  3733.088235
2     Gentoo  5076.016260

title: Palmer Penguins with R and Python
text:
Visualize the result in Python

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.bar(
    average_mass["species"],
    average_mass["body_mass_g"]
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Average body mass (g)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Average penguin body mass calculated from data prepared in R and visualized in Python.

title: Palmer Penguins with R and Python
text:
Findings
The data were first prepared in R and then passed to Python for further analysis. Python calculated the average body mass for each species and created the visualization. Gentoo penguins had the highest average body mass.
